en: Death in a flood of water occurs unpredictably; it does not happen invariably.
However, for humans in the flood of afflictions, untimely death exists without a doubt.
For one fallen into a flood of water, suffering may arise in the mind or it may not.
For one fallen into the flood of afflictions, there is incomparable suffering of both body and mind.
A river whose waters are agitated by its current might sometimes and perhaps lead to the ocean;
but the river of craving drags one toward the ocean of saṃsāra, which is even beyond the ocean.
A mountain river reaches its full capacity with the arrival of the clouds; yet, even by vast waters, it never attains satisfaction— just as the river of craving is never satiated by sense objects.
In which there is neither birth, nor old age, nor disease, nor death;
no union with the unpleasant, nor separation from the pleasant;
and no failure to obtain the desired object.
That alone is considered happiness by me; I know everything else to be suffering.
Even having reached the far shore of the ocean of manifold doubt, there would still be the suffering of wild beasts, fire, kings, and thieves.
But having reached the further shore of the waters of the ocean of saṃsāra, there is not even the slightest suffering; rather, there is supreme peace. 27.1.8 [...]
Just as a physician, having correctly understood the state of a patient's constitution, prescribes beneficial medicinal regimens for the purpose of exhausting diseases; so too [the Buddha],
having understood the diverse natures of sentient beings as they reside within their mental dispositions...

In the same way, the Buddha spoke the Dharma as if it were medicine. §1 Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:

§2 “Monks, it is just as if a great multitude of people were being carried along with the current of a river of caustic liquid, whose banks are glowing embers, whose bed is strewn with thorns, which is blind, and which is a blinding, pitch-black darkness.”

In that situation, suppose there were a certain being who was not of a foolish nature, not of a deluded nature, but of a wise nature; one who desired happiness and was averse to suffering, who desired life and did not desire death, and who was averse to dying. It would occur to him: "Why indeed should I be carried along with the current by this river of caustic brine, whose banks are filled with glowing embers, whose bed is strewn with thorns, which is blind, dark, and shrouded in blinding gloom? What if I were to exert myself against the current with my hands and feet?"
Having reflected thus, he exerts himself even more intensely with his hands and feet against the current.

There he might see a light. It would occur to him: "A great darkness has been overcome by this distinction, namely, this light. What if I were to exert myself even more intensely with my hands and feet against the current? Having reflected thus, he exerts himself even more intensely with his hands and feet against the current.

There he would see a level stretch of ground; he would stand upon it. Standing there, he would look out in the four directions. There he would see a great mountain, solid, without cracks, without holes, well-rounded, and a single compact mass. He would climb up it.

There he would see water endowed with eight qualities: cool, sweet, light, soft, clear, free from foul odors, which does not irritate the throat when drunk and does not afflict the stomach once swallowed. Having bathed and drunk there, his fever and burning heat gone, he would ascend that very same great mountain.

There he would see seven species of flowers, namely: the blue lotus (*utpala*), the red lotus (*padma*), the night-lotus (*kumuda*), the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), the fragrant lotus (*saugandhika*), the soft-scented lotus (*mṛdugandhika*), and the *atimukta* as the seventh. Sniffing those very seven species of flowers, he would ascend that same great rocky mountain.

There he would see a four-stepped staircase; he would ascend it. There he would see a celestial palace with five pillars; he would enter it. There he would see a couch provided with a cushioned frame, spread with a woolen rug, spread with cotton wool, spread with a thick coverlet, spread with variegated rugs, and spread with fine cloth, covered with a silk canopy, furnished with red pillows at both ends, strewn with various flowers, and delightful.
He might sit down there or lie down there; as he is sitting or lying there, cool breezes would blow upon him from the four directions.

There he would raise his voice and proclaim: "By this way, noble ones; by this way, gentle friends, there is an escape against the current from this river of caustic brine, which has banks of glowing embers, a bed of thorns, and is shrouded in blinding, pitch-black darkness. Others asked: "By which way, noble ones? By which way, gentle friends, is there an escape against the current from this river of caustic brine, which has banks of glowing embers, a bed of thorns, and is blind with blinding, pitch-black darkness?"

Others said this: "Friends, he too does not know; he too does not see; he too is being carried along with the current by this river of caustic liquid, which has banks of glowing embers, a bed of thorns, and is blind, dark, and shrouded in blinding gloom."

§10 Thus, monks, this simile has been made only for the sake of making the meaning known. Furthermore, this is the meaning to be understood here: "Caustic," monks, is a designation for the three types of evil, unwholesome thoughts; namely, the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty. "River," monks, is a designation for the three types of craving; namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.

"Kukūla-kūla" (the burning chaff) is a designation for the six internal sense-bases (*āyatana*). "Darkness and gloom" is a designation for the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*). "A great multitude of people" is a designation for foolish ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*). "A single being who is not of a foolish nature, not of a deluded nature, but of a wise nature" is a designation for the Bodhisattva. "The current" is a designation for the current of saṃsāra. "One would strive against the current with both hands and feet" is a designation for the exertion of vigor (*vīrya*).
"Light" is a designation for the patient acceptance that arises from the contemplation of dharmas.

"A level stretch of ground" is a designation for the precepts. "Looking out in the four directions" is a designation for the four noble truths. "A great rocky mountain" is a designation for right view.

"Water endowed with eight qualities" is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path. "Seven kinds of flowers" is a designation for the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). "A four-pillared staircase" is a designation for the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*). "A five-pillared celestial palace" is a designation for the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

“Cross-legged” is a designation for the realm of nirvana with a remainder of substrate. “Strewed with flowers and delightful” is a designation for the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. “He sits there, having sat down,” is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. “Cool breezes blow from the four directions” is a designation for the four super-mind states that constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life.

"Uttering sound and making a noise" is a designation for the teaching of the Dharma. In this regard, those who say, "By what means, O Noble Ones? By what means, O Blessed-Faced Ones, is there an escape by going against the current from this river of caustic matter, which has banks of glowing embers, a bed of thorns, and is blind, dark, and shrouded in thick gloom?"—this is a designation for the two monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; it is also a designation for the group of the five, the group of the next five, and the assembly of the sixty members of the auspicious troop.
Furthermore, there are others who possess right view and have entered upon the right path.

Among them, those who say, "Friends, even this one does not know; even this one does not see; even this one is being carried along with the current by this river of caustic matter, with banks of glowing embers, strewn with thorns, blind, dark, and shrouded in blinding gloom"—this is a designation for the six teachers.

Namely: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Saṃjayin Vairaṭṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyanīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra; or whoever else there may be who hold wrong views and have entered upon wrong practice. "Thus, monks, that which is to be done for disciples by a teacher who is compassionate, merciful, desirous of their welfare, seeking their benefit, and acting out of pity—that has been done by me. Now, it is for you to do it."

"Monks, these are remote lodgings—forests, the roots of trees, empty huts, mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces, cemeteries, and forest retreats. Meditate, monks; do not be negligent, lest you be full of regret later. This is my instruction. Thus he spoke.
